title: MSPs reject datacentre moratorium but pause planning decisions
raw_text:
The Scottish Parliament this week rejected a Green motion for a moratorium on new hyperscale datacentres, but amended it with a commitment to publish national planning guidance by Christmas, and a Labour clause that freezes planning and consenting decisions until that guidance lands.

The government amendment, put by public finance minister Hannah Mary Goodlad, passed by 72 votes to 32 with 16 abstentions on 16 September. A Labour amendment also passed, inserting text that no decision on planning or consenting should be made until the guidance and strategy are complete.

The outcome left the word “moratorium” off the statute book, but delivered much of the pause campaigners sought by a different route. Goodlad was explicit that she rejected the Greens’ framing. “We do not agree that there should be a moratorium,” she told the chamber. “That is not necessary. It’s not appropriate and it would send the wrong message to anyone looking to invest in Scotland.”

Goodlad’s amendment pledged the “swift creation of national planning and spatial guidance by the end of the year”, and she committed to move faster than Labour’s 12-month timetable. “We’re actually minded to support the Labour amendment today, but we think we can be more ambitious,” she said. “We want to come back with guidance on this in three months’ time, by Christmas.”

Alongside the vote, the minister confirmed a new planning direction requiring an environmental impact assessment for every datacentre application of more than 50MW, applying to new bids and to schemes already in the system. It took effect the following day, and followed an August direction requiring councils to notify ministers within seven days of any application exceeding 50MW.

The scale at stake had grown sharply. Computer Weekly’s analysis of Barbour ABI data put Scotland’s committed pipeline at 14 schemes totalling 2.4GW, up from four projects and 0.9GW in March – the fastest growth of any UK region. That sat inside a UK-wide committed pipeline of 173 schemes and more than 14.6GW.

Campaigners count a far larger number because they tally earlier stages of the process. The Scottish Greens and countryside charity Action to Protect Rural Scotland put the pipeline at 24 proposals with a combined capacity of up to 6GW, which the Greens said was more than 1.5x Scotland’s peak power demand. The gap between 14 committed schemes and 24 claimed proposals is itself a measure of how much of Scotland’s mooted pipeline remained speculative.

  • UK committed datacentre pipeline grows to more than 14GW: Barbour ABI data show the committed UK pipeline has grown to 173 schemes and more than 14.6GW, with Scotland's 14 committed schemes growing faster than anywhere else.
  • Planning for datacentres needs evidence, not guesswork: Why UK digital infrastructure growth needs an evidence-led, transparent planning framework rather than reliance on speculative forecasts.

Labour’s Paul Sweeney, who moved the amendment, framed the question as one of national design rather than developer speculation. “Now we have 15 in Scotland, with 23 proposed,” he said, urging colleagues to build the sector “by national design and not by private speculation”.

Labour’s closing speaker, Monica Lennon, argued communities needed certainty that decisions would not slip through before the guidance arrived. “We need to have a pause to get that robust guidance,” she said. Goodlad countered that a standstill was effectively in place already: “It is highly unlikely that we will see decisions taken before Christmas.”

The amended motion imposed no statutory moratorium, so a council could in principle still consent a scheme before Christmas. Green MSP Mark Ruskell warned that three hyperscale applications were likely to be determined this year, including the Larbert site in Falkirk, where a pre-determination hearing took place on the night of the vote and the determination deadline was 4 October.

Pressure for a halt to datacentre projects has built since the summer, when the SNP’s national council backed a moratorium and Goodlad began intervening in individual schemes, such as ordering environmental impact assessments at Wester Hermiston and Auchtertool. The National Planning Framework 4 designation of “green datacentres” as priority developments sat at the heart of the fight, because the term still carries no binding definition. 

For datacentre developers and the enterprise buyers that depend on them, the vote sent a mixed signal. It kept the door open to the UK’s fastest-growing datacentre market, but replaced the certainty of a moratorium with the uncertainty of a promise – guidance by Christmas, and no consenting decisions until it lands.

title: CW@60: Six stories for sixty years
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

Computer Weekly’s 60th anniversary is a great opportunity to reflect on what we have learned - and possibly not learned - about the positive contribution different technologies have made to work and life in general.

In each of Computer Weekly’s six decades there have been breakthroughs which have been greeted with positive and negative reactions. Reflecting on six symbolic technology stories that have emerged during each of the past six decades, I suggest there are lessons for us today as we consider the next disruptive innovation that is artificial intelligence (AI).

Story 1: The 1960s - the calculator

The first electronic calculators started appearing in the 1960s and the prototype of the portable calculator, the “Cal Tech,” was revealed by Texas Instruments. Technically, they didn’t go mainstream until the 1970s, but the response from educators and policy makers was interesting. In the US, a report by the National Advisory Committee on Mathematical Education in 1975 said that all US students over the age of 13/14 should have access to calculators for class work and exams.

By 1986, a group of US teachers was protesting against the use of calculators. In the UK in 2014, the government banned the use of calculators for 11-year-olds in a national maths test. However, by 2018 research from the Education Endowment Foundation suggested that calculators can “boost pupils’ fluency and understanding of maths.”

Today, we’ve reached a more balanced view that calculators can aid learning, but students still need a strong grounding in the “rules” of mathematics to understand how to get the most value from a calculator.

Story 2: The 1970s - the start of the video game era

This decade saw the commercialisation of the video games industry with the arrival of Atari in 1972. By 1974, Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak had developed Breakout and in 1976, Atari was sold to Warner Communications for a mere $28m to continue funding the Video Computer System.

“We are at a major inflection point where there is understandably a lot of concern and excitement about AI’s potential impact. I would argue that it is not the technology that is the problem, but how certain people might use it”

Simon Paris

Perhaps at the time, it might have been difficult to envision how embedded gaming would become in our lives, but in 2025, Statista estimated that revenue from the global gaming industry was almost $522.5bn.

This is where you begin to realise the power of technology - how it could move out of the calculator into something in your home. It also flags its adaptability and flexibility. Atari went on to introduce the Atari Home Computer System in 1979. Perhaps not quite as catchy a name as the version two former employees, Jobs and Wozniak, went on to build but it showed technology can open up new opportunities. It just requires rule breakers and risk takers, willing to stake their reputations on something that not everyone can imagine.

Story 3: The 1980s - consumer electronics takes off

Aside from personal computers becoming a thing in the 1980s, the Sony Walkman and the VHS player emerged. Again, these technologies are a long way off the likes of Spotify and Netflix, but they gave consumers choice about how, when or where they listened or watched. This is exemplified by the birth of the mobile phone. On 21 September 1983 Motorola launched the first commercially available DynaTAC 8000X.

Perhaps more interesting, though, is the journey of the mobile phone. The telephone aspect is almost the last thing we associate with them these days. They have become an irreplaceable life assistant. They give users agency emphasising their utility and ability to offer unexpected value.

Story 4: The 1990s - the rise of digital banking

The concept of home banking emerged in the 1980s, but it wasn’t until the late 1990s that the likes of Barclays Bank introduced the UK’s first online banking service. We are still only at the beginning of that impact with challenger banks like Revolut and e-trading platforms. What I find interesting is how society and the financial services industry has reacted to technology change.

When I worked at McKinsey, I had a clear objective to introduce technology that would help to automate and eliminate mundane tasks, but from the appearance of the first ATM there has always been some push back.

Would customers be comfortable using machines rather than going into branches? Telephone banking further shifted the focus away from the local branch and was accelerated by the arrival of self-service banking.

Yes, this has disrupted the way banks serve customers which has had consequences for roles within retail banking, but it has also increased convenience and given consumers more choice in how they engage with banks.

This is where technology can have a profound positive effect on human enablement and agency even for demographics who may be slower to embrace digital technologies. With a guided, assisted approach retail banks have opened up these new capabilities to a wide range of customers.

Story 5: The 2000s - overcoming (very) personal barriers

This story is more how technology had a deeply positive impact for our family. My daughter was born deaf, but in this decade at the age of just two she received two cochlear implants. This is one example of how embedded technologies used in healthcare can improve outcomes. Today my daughter is a bilingual graduate, living, working in and travelling to multiple countries, fully participating in life.

It is quite humbling to consider how technology, as it becomes pervasive, can make such a positive contribution to society. At Unit4, we see that every day working with organisations in public services, higher education and non-profit sectors. Technology gives volunteers and educators time back to do the work that matters most.

Story 6: The 2010s and 2020s

The story that stands out to me in more recent decades is how some core technologies have matured – I’m thinking particularly of cloud computing, and what that has meant for more recent innovations like AI and autonomous technologies, as well as reducing the cost and barrier to entry to a whole world of entrepreneurship.

As a result, we are now at a major inflection point where there is understandably a lot of concern and excitement about its potential impact. In the case of AI, I would argue that it is not the technology that is the problem, but perhaps how certain people might use it.

Technology is not inherently “evil” or malicious, whereas a bad human actor might lead it to be. There is definitely a need for guardrails and regulation, but as with speed limits on the motorway there will always be those who knowingly break the rules, whatever rules we put in place.  

Conclusion

What the last 60 years has taught me is that when we make technology human-centric, enabling and empowering users to access its utility, it can have surprising and positive life-changing effects on individuals and on society. Benefits that the original designers may not even have expected.

History teaches us that we require technologists willing to take risks.

Regulation and guardrails will be in place to protect us, but in reality it will not prevent some people trying to do bad things. As a result, technology-enabled change can be uncomfortable.

However, if we understand that our relationship with technology is a journey with no end destination because technology will continuously evolve, then I believe pervasive access to innovation can drive wonderful outcomes including equality, equity, inclusion, empowerment, entrepreneurship, health, education – the list is endless. And yes, I am an optimist.

In the coming 60 years we’ll continue to see technology help society to progress by giving users agency. A farmer in a remote community increasing their knowhow around yield and crop management just as easily as a well-established farming operation is a great equaliser. This agency is a powerful force for positive change.

Oh, and happy 60th birthday Computer Weekly - thanks for keeping us so informed over all these years.

Simon Paris is chief executive officer at Unit4.

title: GISEC Global highlights growing influence of women leaders in cyber resilience
raw_text:
As governments and organisations across the Middle East accelerate investments in cyber resilience, industry leaders increasingly recognise that effective security programmes require more than technology alone. Diverse leadership teams, access to strategic opportunities and inclusive workplace cultures are emerging as critical factors in strengthening organisational cyber defences.

The issue is particularly relevant in the Gulf region, where national cyber security strategies and digital transformation initiatives are driving growing demand for skilled professionals who can manage increasingly complex threat environments.

While the cyber security industry has made progress in attracting more women into the profession, many leaders argue that the conversation should now shift from representation to opportunity. The challenge is no longer whether women can succeed in cyber security, but whether they have access to the high-profile projects, critical infrastructure programmes and leadership roles that ultimately shape future executives.

“Leadership comes from experience,” said Yuliana Martirosyan, senior director and head of application security at Visa. “If you don’t get those most challenging projects, it’s very difficult to get that experience to get you to the next level.”

According to Martirosyan, organisations must actively create pathways into these opportunities, while individuals must also be willing to take on unfamiliar and demanding responsibilities.

Cyber security leaders also highlighted the growing importance of diverse perspectives in addressing modern threats. As cyber attacks become more sophisticated and interconnected, organisations increasingly benefit from teams that bring different experiences, backgrounds and approaches to risk management.

Arianna Lepore, from the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), argued that organisations often focus too heavily on gender comparisons rather than on the value that diverse teams bring to cyber resilience. “The broader the composition of teams, the broader the experience and the approach to threat, the better the responses are,” she said.

Creating environments where talent can thrive is equally important. Industry experts noted that many young women entering cyber security possess the necessary technical skills and qualifications but often lack opportunities to demonstrate their expertise or gain visibility within organisations.

“What young women are missing is the space – not the competencies, not the capacities, not the self-confidence, but the space,” said Lepore.

This emphasis on creating opportunities aligns closely with the UAE’s wider efforts to develop cyber security capabilities. Through initiatives led by government entities, universities and industry events, the country has invested heavily in developing local cyber talent and encouraging greater participation across the sector.

Industry communities also play a key role. Lena Yu, a cyber security analyst and researcher, highlighted the importance of building environments where professionals feel safe to contribute and where inappropriate behaviour is challenged.

“One of the hardest parts is having the strength and courage to hold bad personalities accountable,” she said. “If there is no one to hold them accountable, they will keep doing it.”

For many female leaders, however, the biggest obstacles are not always organisational. Several pointed to confidence and self-perception as barriers that can prevent talented professionals from pursuing leadership positions.

Reflecting on her own career, Lepore said she spent years waiting for permission to contribute before realising that the limitation was largely self-imposed.

“I was waiting for permission to sit at the table and contribute,” Yu said. “It was myself that I was waiting for permission from.”

Such experiences resonate across the cyber security profession, where rapid technological change often requires professionals to step outside their comfort zone and continuously adapt to new challenges. For Eng.Huda Ahmed Mohsen, chief of information technology at Bahrain’s Ministry of Information, the focus should remain firmly on capability and performance rather than gender.

“I’m focusing on my capabilities, my achievements and my leadership,” she said. “Focus on the output.”

As the Middle East continues to strengthen its cyber security posture, leaders increasingly agree that resilience depends not only on technology investments but also on ensuring that the industry’s best talent has the opportunity to develop, contribute and lead.

title: CW@60: Sixty years of hurt, hope, and high technology
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

If you were born between 1965 and 1980 then you are from Generation X - this is my generation and it’s also when Computer Weekly was born, in 1966.

Douglas Coupland celebrated Generation X by creating a 1990s version of The Canterbury Tales, but others may remember the punk band Gen X, fronted by Billy Idol and Tony James.

There is an enormous amount of nostalgia for 1966. It’s the only year that the England men’s team has ever won the football World Cup. This summer, we all sang ”60 years of hurt” and lost again.

Michael Calvin’s book 1966: A moment in time reveals a more challenging time than Facebook nostalgia ever would allow.

The UK still faced strong class division that is in contrast to the popular image of the “swinging sixties”. Racism was structural and normalised - also symbolised by FIFA only allocating one place at the World Cup Finals for all of Asia, Oceania, and Africa. The Africans just boycotted the cup.

Time travel

But in technology, the period since 1966 has been transformative. A time traveller from the 1960s would not recognise our world. Star Trek IV: The voyage home featured our favourite space explorers from the 23rd century returning to 1980s California and being dumbfounded that they could not speak to a computer.

In 2026, my four-year-old daughter knows she can say, “Alexa, play Harry Styles” when she wants some sounds.

The room-sized computing systems of the 1970s developed into PCs and then a global cloud-based ecosystem. British computer scientist Tim Berners-Lee was instrumental in creating the World Wide Web at CERN. The ARM chip architecture, created by Acorn in Cambridge, now powers most of the mobile devices we are using today.

“When I started in banking technology, I was coding trading ideas - we even called one arbitrage app ‘Bonanza’ because the advice it gave was like a licence to print money”

Mark Hillary

My father marvels that he can talk on video to his granddaughter in São Paulo, from his home in Dorset, entirely free using WhatsApp. In the 1960s this type of voice call was just about possible, but would involve booking a three-minute slot, which may involve waiting for hours, and then paying hundreds of dollars for that brief connection.

Scottish inventor James Goodfellow patented the plastic bank card and PIN system in 1966 and a year later the first ATM in the world opened at Barclays Bank in Enfield. Today, I use PIX for most of my financial transactions, from paying my electricity bill to paying a friend back for a round in the pub.

Witness to a wild ride

Personally, I have witnessed the birth of the web, the introduction of email, the arrival of social media, and the more recent introduction of consumer-facing artificial intelligence. It’s been a wild ride and I’ve been lucky to work inside - or adjacent to - the technology industry all this time.

I studied A-level computer science and then software engineering and I still have many of my old textbooks. It’s impossible to find “internet” or “www” mentioned in the index of any of these books, which now seems bizarre. It’s like some prehistoric era.

I can’t think of any other industry that would have afforded me so many opportunities in the time that I have been working professionally in technology - or the ability to witness so much industrial change up close.

I was teaching kids how to code and control robots in Washington DC in the early 1990s. I designed the software that went into the Siemens Nixdorf checkouts of Tesco and Dixons - I even personally designed the bitmap of the Dixons logo that was printed on every 1990s receipt. 

I was lucky enough to work on trading floors in the City of London during the 1990s - before automated trading killed the atmosphere of working on a busy trading desk.

When I started in banking technology, I was coding trading ideas - we even called one arbitrage app “Bonanza” because the advice it gave was like a licence to print money. Eventually I became a technology director, leading the team that kept my bank connected to stock exchanges globally.

My business travel schedule back then was absurd. Every week I was somewhere new. It’s why I always ignore “travel influencers” who say, “I have visited 13 countries.” Come and talk to me when you lost count at 100.

Becoming a ghost

Computing and Computer Weekly magazines were significant in my career change to writing about technology - the connecting thread being that editor-in-chief Bryan Glick was previously at Computing.

I wrote a book about the rise of the technology industry in India in 2004. I left the bank because I had a publishing contract for the book and I had a few articles commenting on tech published in major newspapers. It felt like I could switch to writing professionally.

But even then, it was not easy to get noticed as a writer. Computing, and then subsequently Computer Weekly, gave me my own column and this led to me becoming a tech-focused ghostwriter - ghosting for senior leaders in companies such as BT and TCS, and for the government too. My favourite ghosting experience was talking to Neil Armstrong in person and helping him insert jokes into his standard “going to the moon” speech.

In 2026, Computer Weekly is still going strong and has had enormous recognition recently for the role the magazine played in uncovering the British Post Office Horizon software scandal.

I’m also still writing about technology - I just published my 29th book. I’ve written books for the British Computer Society and the UN, alongside some of my own pet projects. I’m also still ghosting for leaders all over the world. I just can’t say who they are.

Happy birthday to Computer Weekly for a memorable 60 years and for helping me to switch from managing technology systems to writing about them.

title: Saffron Building Society drinks its ‘first drop’ of artificial intelligence
raw_text:
Saffron Building Society is using artificial intelligence (AI) to automate mortgage processing and increase “decision certainty” for its brokers.

The 180-year-old Essex-based mutual society has penned a deal with FintechOS to use the supplier’s AI platform and is getting started with its residential mortgage processing business.

The company plans to double its mortgage lending to £2bn over the next five years and so needed to increase its processing capacity through removing manual processes through AI.

Qasir Aslam, chief transformation officer at the company, described the residential mortgage project as being the company’s “first drop” into the IT platform as his team seeks to prove the value of AI on a case-by-case basis.

Changing expectations

The mutual society, which has approximately 200 staff with around 35 in the transformation team, is attempting to meet changing customer and broker expectations. The company sells all its mortgages via brokers, who require a clear understanding of the company’s offerings, while customers require a smooth process.

“From a broker perspective, they want to understand what our products are and who the customers are – then they need decision certainty,” Aslam told Computer Weekly. “Once information is submitted to us, how quickly can we get back to them with a decision principle and how quickly can we go from the offer to completion?”

Saffron deals with mortgages that are considered complicated. This includes customers who may not have an employment history, or their financial information might not be as straightforward.

“This could be self-employed people, it could be individuals or professionals who they don’t have their regular income, or it could be landlords, for example,” explained Aslam.

“When we implement our new platform, we want to make sure that we’re asking the right questions up-front at application capture, so that when we come back with the decision in principle, brokers have the confidence that it will go through.”

Staff at Saffron will interface with an AI agent known as DAX, with plans to also make this available to brokers. Aslam added: “Colleagues can ask DAX questions, but the plan going forward is then to make that available to brokers as well. If brokers want to understand something specific around a product and a customer, they could ask that agent.”

Aslam described Saffron’s plans to use the platform on a case-by-case basis: “We are going to create a continuous improvement work stream. As part of that, we’re looking at all the processing that we’ve got now, which isn’t optimised, and then looking at what tools are available to help us improve it. That’s where we’ll then look at whether AI will become one of those applicable tools for us.”

Drop by drop

This “drop-by-drop” approach, according to Aslam, will help his team prove the value of AI in use cases to the business: “The biggest challenge, based on my experience of implementing lots of these platforms, is making sure that we can implement something quickly that shows to the wider business the value that the platform can deliver.

“What I am trying to do with the business areas is [uncover] what the first drop of value that we can go and deploy early next year [is], so that we can demonstrate delivery success and show how great this platform is. We then want to iteratively build on it. Once we’ve deployed our first release, our first drop of value, we can add more products onto the platform.

“With residential mortgage origination, we want to lay the foundations so that the end-to-end application journey, the mortgage lifecycle, is on FintechOS. Once it’s live, we’ll learn a lot more about the platform and how we use the platform, then optimise and make it even more efficient,” added Aslam.

He said that while a company of Saffron’s size cannot match the processing efficiencies of its large competitors, “where we identify a process is broken, we’ll be able to vastly improve those”.

Aslam said the company had to ensure its staff came on the AI journey with the company: “The first thing we needed to do was reassure them. We’ve been clear from a Saffron perspective that when we look at AI, we’re going to make sure it’s human centric.

“The way I explain it to everybody is that AI isn’t there to take your job away. AI is there to help you to automate the mundane, day-to-day tasks so that you can focus on more value add.”

He said value add is about having time to go and speak to brokers, understand what their points are, and understand how to improve products. “That’s where we want to move the workforce and where they spend a lot of their brain power,” he said.

The use of AI is being emulated and encouraged across the mortgage sector.

Earlier this year, Vernon Building Society described its use of FintechOS, stating that it can now compete with big mortgage providers on the speed of mortgage processing, while ensuring its people focus on how it differentiates.

The Stockport-based company, which has 25,000 members and total assets of around £534m, specialises in savings and more complex mortgages. The firm is growing, with a 4.6% increase in mortgages on its books, now worth £439.5m, a 5.4% increase in total assets from last year.

Separately, in December 2025, as part of its plan to build the “mortgage market of the future”, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) outlined four areas of focus.

One of these, which looks at innovation and disclosure, will increase the use of AI among brokers while preserving humans in the process, according to the FCA. It said it is “encouraging the use of data and technology, such as AI, to help brokers give better and faster advice while keeping a human touch”.

title: CW@60: Sixty years of progress - but still not everyone's invited
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

I've spent years watching the same technology hand one person their independence back and lock another person out of the door.

Screen readers and voice assistants have given blind and low-vision people independence that simply didn't exist a generation ago. Robotics and powered prosthetics have changed what mobility means for people with limb differences. Healthtech, from remote monitoring to AI-assisted diagnostics, is catching conditions earlier and keeping people out of hospital who would once have had no choice but to be in one.

I've watched all of it change real lives, and it's a large part of why I still do this work.

However, for all of this progress there is an unevenness in how that progress lands. It doesn't arrive as a rising tide that lifts everyone together - it arrives at different speeds for different people.

For some of us the pace is thrilling - a new app, a new assistant, a new diagnostic tool, all within months of each other. For others it's more like Swiss cheese, patches of real progress with enormous holes in between. If you're standing in one of those holes, the fact that the cheese exists at all is cold comfort.

What the holes look like

Take GP appointments. Healthwatch England, the statutory NHS and social care watchdog, found that only 30% of patients are always given a choice of how they book - phone, in person or online - and 16% are never given that choice at all, despite the GP contract explicitly guaranteeing it.

The gap hits older people and disabled patients hardest. Separately, the charity Re-engage found that a third of people aged 75 and over can only get a GP appointment if they book digitally, and 70% said they lacked the equipment or skills to do so without help. Its report describes the shift as leaving older patients feeling "discriminated against" and "dehumanised."

There is a gap - it's not whether the nuts and bolts of the technology work, because so often they work brilliantly, but whether the system built around it was designed with the person standing in front of it in mind. The tools can be extraordinary for those who were counted in to the design. The systems wrapped around them too often aren't designed for the assumed user, rolled out at speed, with no fallback for anyone who doesn't fit.

Every generation gets a new gate

When I started working in this sector, the industry loved the language of revolution - disruption, transformation, the future arriving all at once. What nobody said out loud was that the future arrived unevenly, on a schedule set by income, geography, and who the designers pictured when they imagined a "user."

In early meetings, that user was, without anyone quite admitting it, a specific person - connected, sighted, often male, English speaking, able to afford the latest device. Everyone else was an edge case, something to "get to later." Later rarely came on schedule.

Part of that comes down to who's actually in the room when these decisions get made. Women are significantly underrepresented in the UK's tech workforce, and the gap widens further for disabled technologists and people from lower-income backgrounds - the exact groups most likely to be treated as edge cases rather than users.

I've sat in plenty of rooms where I was the only woman, and I've watched how that shapes what gets built and what gets deferred. It's not that anyone in those rooms meant harm. It's that a team that all shares the same daily experience of technology will, without noticing, design for that experience and call it universal.

“I still believe in what technology can do. What I've stopped believing is that any of that has to be left to chance, decided by who happened to be in the room, who could afford the device, who fit the assumption. Inclusion is the power to make sure it isn't chance”

Karen Blake

Each leap in capability draws a new line between those inside the gate and those still trying to find it, and the line tends to fall in the same place, again and again, because the room deciding where to put it rarely changes.

But the room isn't fixed, and the work to change it is already underway. What we need now is pace. Change happens the moment someone with power in the room chooses to use it differently, and that responsibility doesn't only sit with engineers, it sits with all of us.

The tech industry holds a disproportionate share of that power, especially in the roles that shape a product before the public ever sees it - procurement teams who can specify accessibility as a contract requirement, not a nice-to-have. Commissioners who can refuse to sign off a service until it's tested with the people it will serve. Service design leads who can build the fallback in at the blueprint stage, not bolt one on after the complaints start.

I've seen one person, asking one blunt question at the right moment, stop a flawed product before it ever reached the public. That's proof the shift is possible. What's missing is scale - enough of those questions, asked routinely enough, that raising the floor becomes the standard, not the exception. That takes perspective, commitment, and consistency. Let's make sure the algorithm counts people in, rather than out.

The trap of ‘inevitability’

"Well, everyone has a smartphone now." Everyone doesn't. Nor does everyone have a reliable connection or literacy to use it. But once enough people say it, it becomes true by policy. Services move online, paper forms disappear, and not having the device stops being an inconvenience and becomes exclusion from healthcare, benefits, school, work.

This is the shape of inevitability - technology doesn't just get adopted, it gets assumed. Once assumed, the people who fall outside it stop being visible as a design problem and start being blamed as a personal failing.

"You should just learn." As if the barrier were their unwillingness, rather than a system that never asked if they could get through the door.

Who actually agreed to this?

There's a feeling I keep encountering - in community halls, in patient groups, with fellow technologists - that AI is a runaway train. Not something being built, with choices at every junction, but something already moving, already decided, that the rest of us can only board or be left behind by. That feeling deserves more scrutiny than it gets.

Inevitability is a story, and it's one the industry tells more often than it questions - that AI will reshape every part of our lives regardless of whether anyone actually agreed to it.

Nobody I've spoken to remembers being asked. Not about their GP surgery, not about their bank, not about the care plan drawn up for their elderly parent. What they remember is being informed, after the fact, that the route had already been chosen.

Right now there's real momentum around being first to adopt AI, and being fast is treated as its own virtue, as if speed were evidence of quality. But a runaway train doesn't ask where you wanted to go. Collective consent - real, ongoing, informed agreement from the communities affected - is the thing missing, and it's worth asking why we've allowed speed to stand in for it.

It doesn't have to work that way. I keep coming back to what it would look like if communities had a genuine, ongoing voice in their own technology - not just a survey after the fact, but real influence over whether a tool gets built at all, how it's tested, and what happens to the people it doesn't work for.

Moreover, my concern is where that testing actually happens. When we try to prove out productivity gains, the proving ground is too often services used disproportionately by underserved communities, GP surgeries, social care, benefits systems, exactly the places where people have the least power to say no, and the least capacity to absorb it when the tool gets it wrong. Efficiency gets demonstrated on the people who can least afford to be the demonstration.

Consent, done properly, isn't a box ticked once in a policy document nobody reads. It's an ongoing conversation about what a community actually wants technology to do for them. The train only feels unstoppable because so few people have been asked to weigh in on where it's headed, and the more people insist on being asked, the less inevitable the destination becomes.

We know more than we used to

Technology keeps changing costume, but the question underneath it hasn't moved - who is this built for, and who is left behind when the pace is speedy for some and Swiss cheese for others?

Inclusion isn't the finishing touch on a technology landscape. It's the thing that decides whether that landscape is worth building in the first place. A tool that only works for the person it was designed around isn't neutral, it's just narrow - and narrow tools eventually fail everyone, because none of us stay inside the assumed default forever. We age. We acquire disabilities. We lose signal, lose income, lose the version of ourselves the system was built for. A landscape designed for genuine inclusion isn't a kindness extended to the few. It's the only version of progress sturdy enough to hold all of us.

That landscape doesn't get built by accident, and it doesn't get built by one sector alone. It doesn't require a different 60 years. It requires more people, in more rooms, refusing to treat exclusion as the acceptable cost of speed.

I still believe in what technology can do. I've seen it hand people back their independence, their mobility, their time. What I've stopped believing is that any of that has to be left to chance, decided by who happened to be in the room, who could afford the device, who fit the assumption.

Inclusion is the power to make sure it isn't chance. It's ours to use, and it's ours to keep using, together, on purpose, for as long as this technology keeps changing shape.

Karen Blake is a member of the UK government’s Women in Tech Taskforce and co-author of the Lovelace report investigating why so many women leave the tech sector.

title: Tech companies under fire as Europe proposes social media ban for under-15s
raw_text:
Children under 15 in Europe will be prohibited from having unsupervised social media accounts, along with new demands for technology companies to prove their platforms are safe.

European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen told a State of the Union address at the European Parliament that Europe intended to “reverse the burden of proof” for the safety of children onto technology companies. “Platforms will have to prove to us that they are safe,” she said. “Because it is not about our minors accessing social media. It is about when and how do we allow social media to access minors.”

The EU Kids Act, to be published tomorrow, will ban children under 13 from social media entirely, and children under 15 will be limited to accounts controlled by their parents, with access restricted to one hour a day.

Technology companies will be required to provide services that are “safe by design” for children between 15 and 18.

Von der Leyen said she disagreed with the suggestion it was impossible to roll back the “overwhelming” power of big tech companies. “Europe has the power to act,” she said. “It is we who decide our rules, not big tech. We do not have to accept addictive features. We do not have to accept children being drawn into ever more extreme content. We do not have to accept that girls have their photos used for AI-generated sexualised images.”

According to a draft of the proposed regulation seen by Computer Weekly, the proposals extend beyond social media companies. Video-sharing services, online games, chatbots and app stores will also be required to follow “safety by design” requirements, including verifying the age of users.

The draft has raised concerns among some critics that it would lead to the widespread use of “identity checkpoints” on internet services to verify people’s ages, changing the “open nature” of online services.

Children deprived of childhood

Von der Leyen said it was necessary to take steps as children were spending four to six hours a day on their screens and being pulled in by algorithms designed to keep them scrolling. That was leading to loss of sleep, anxiety and even self-harm.

“What we are witnessing is a great capture of our children,” she said. “A capture of their attention, their focus, their minds. This is depriving children of their childhood.”

The EU’s move will introduce a single approach across EU member states to regulating social media and other online services accessed by children, in the wake of proposals by Italy, France, Norway, Greece, Austria, Poland and Belgium to introduce their own social media bans.

It follows Australia, the first country to ban social media for young people in December 2025, and the UK’s announcement of a social media ban for under-16s in June 2026, which requires tech companies to introduce age verification.

Identity checkpoints challenge open internet

James Baker, a manager at campaign organisation Open Rights Group, told Computer Weekly that drafts of the EU Kids Act extended online ID checks across social media, to app stores, games and other services.

“Our concern is that this changes the fundamental open nature of the internet and makes it a permission-based system where you are required to pass through an identity checkpoint to access information,” he said.

Baker said the proposals could also adversely impact small service providers and community-run projects attempting to provide alternatives to Big Tech. “Imposing the same complex compliance requirements on those services risks pushing them out,” said Baker.

Isabelle Roccia, managing director for Europe at the International Association of Privacy Professionals, said the European Commission’s proposals raised complex questions over what level of risk was acceptable in online services. j

“The EU Kids Act will raise very real governance questions for operators in scope, [including] how to cater to age categories when designing and delivering services,” she said.

Other challenges included “how to navigate the complex interplay of existing laws and guardrails with this extra layer of protection; and how to untangle the chain of responsibility, accountability and duty-of-care in an online environment where these concepts are still fairly new”, she said.

title: Why Thomson Reuters developed its own proprietary AI model
raw_text:
Financial information provider Thomson Reuters has developed an in-house, proprietary large language model (LLM) to power its use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the products it develops for customers.

Senior executives in most major enterprises are turning to generative and agentic AI to explore value-generating opportunities – but significant challenges, such as security, accuracy and fears over supplier lock-in, can prevent firms from making the most of such opportunities.

In a pioneering attempt to overcome these issues, content and technology specialist Thomson Reuters has taken a step that would be anathema to many CIOs and their C-suite colleagues – launching its own in-house-developed proprietary LLM.

Kirsty Roth, chief operating officer at Thomson Reuters, understands that many of her digital leadership peers would see the company’s decision to launch its LLM, known as Thomson, as radical. Tech giants, such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, spend billions of dollars developing new models on what feels like a weekly release cadence.

AI model development is a world characterised by rapid change and high investment, so why would a traditional blue-chip enterprise outside the high-tech world of super-powerful frontier models decide to spend millions of dollars developing its own LLM? After all, aren’t the tech giants always going to be bigger and better at AI?

Not necessarily, suggests Roth. Yes, the behemoths will have the edge in developing publicly available models, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, that a broad user base can explore and exploit for day-to-day activities across a range of industries and professions.

“The big tech companies are always going to be bigger, and I think potentially better for very generic use cases,” she says. “If you’re looking at employee productivity, there’s absolutely no point in us trying to beat that capability. There are millions of users out there for them to capture, and that’s really what they’re focused on.”

However, Thomson Reuters believes the general nature of these frontier models also provides an opportunity for companies to develop LLMs that serve a specific niche. And that’s where the company sees a gap for its new model.

“The challenge is that we operate in quite specific verticals, such as legal and tax, and that’s typically not where the big LLMs are focused,” says Roth.

“Our customers want 99.9% accuracy. They don’t want an 80/20 answer. It was clear that a more focused model had the potential to be better for specific tasks than a generic LLM.”

Blending approaches

Roth explains that Thomson will be plugged into the firm’s in-house developed products for customers in key sectors, such as tax and legal. Rather than calling frontier models to answer a user prompt, as they might have in the past, these products will now call Thomson.

“We wanted to give our customers much more accuracy,” she says. “We wanted to give them the best quality content, at the end of the day. And we felt that if we had our own model, we would be able to do that.”

Roth says the decision to develop an LLM might seem radical to outsiders, but it has been an internal priority for some time. Thomson Reuters acquired UK-based AI startup Safe Sign Technologies in August 2024 with one eye on the future.

“We acquired Safe Sign with a view that, over time, we would learn to train a legal model better than the big frontier labs – not because we’re better than them necessarily, but because this is the specialist area we’re much more focused on, and we want to provide a much narrower set of answers,” she says.

“The way that we can build products now means, yes, we still have people involved, of course, but we can have AI write a large amount of our codebase”

Kirsty Roth, Thomson Reuters

At the time of the acquisition, Thomson Reuters suggested that allying Safe Sign’s developments in legal-specific models with its internal content would help its engineers to deliver high-performing AI solutions.

Two years later, this process has come to fruition with the launch of Thomson. Roth says Safe Sign’s mix of technological and legal expertise is helping her firm to create a competitive advantage.

“If you’re an attorney or tax professional, getting something general that an engineer has created that’s never operated in your business is not necessarily helpful,” she says.

“However, getting a product that’s been built by practitioners, who know how you operate, what your workflows look like, and the way in which you think through a task, means you’re going to get to a much better product. That blend is why this approach made sense for us.”

Counting costs

Now, a warning for CIOs who might be thinking of making a similarly radical move: developing your own LLM isn’t cheap. In addition to buying Safe Sign and investing in its own internal development processes, Thomson Reuters, which built its LLM on an open-source foundation, has invested $40m in training Thomson.

Perhaps unsurprisingly for anyone familiar with LLM technology, Roth says training is the key to AI model success. Thomson has been trained on decades of Thomson Reuters’ proprietary content and domain expertise. And training costs can quickly rack up when you’re developing an LLM.

“It’s really a case of how much training you want to give a model,” she says. “To give you a sense of the cost, a single training run could be $400,000, so that’s why you get to these orders of magnitude quite quickly, because you are still using somebody else’s cloud resource to do that training.”

While the model-development process hasn’t been cheap, Roth suggests it gives Thomson Reuters some key long-term advantages.

First, the model has been trained on the firm’s specialist knowledge, meaning Roth and her team can offer customers bespoke AI services that run on data they already know and trust.

“We believe we have the best content source for legal and tax in the world,” she says. “Therefore, we also believe it would be very hard for anyone else to train the model. If you want evidence for this confidence, the fact that customers in these sectors already want to buy our content tells us quite a lot about how valuable it is.”

Second, Thomson Reuters fully controls its model, without the heavy inference costs of typical frontier models.

“Because Thomson is smaller than a traditional LLM, it’s less latent,” she says. “It tends to work quicker because it’s not searching as many things, and it tends to be cheaper to run because we own it. We’re not relying on third parties, all of whom have profit margins.”

Developing products

The company is already putting its model to work. Thomson’s first deployment is inside Tabular Analysis in CoCounsel Legal, the firm’s AI assistant that helps legal professionals manage research, drafting and document analysis. Roth explains how the deployment works.

“If you are an attorney, and you need to do a huge piece of due diligence with an awful lot of documents, and you want to get a simple view of everything that’s going on and start analysing it, AI can be a fabulous help,” she says.

“Tabular Analysis will get through the work and get you an answer far more quickly, with the accuracy you require.”

While the model has launched publicly, the firm’s developments remain a work in progress. The model has been trained on less than 10% of Thomson Reuters content. Roth says more features will come and it’s important to progress carefully.

“We will add more content as we go into the next versions,” she says. “Early on, to be candid, you don’t know how much money you want to spend because you don’t know how good it is. Now, we’re all building a lot more confidence that this model could be a jewel in the crown.”

Currently, internal engineers use Thomson to develop products. However, Roth recognises there is the long-term potential for the firm to sell its model to outside enterprises, including law firms that could use the LLM to question their own data sources securely.

“We have not yet said we’re going to go and sell Thomson,” she says. “As you can probably imagine, there’s quite a lot of interest. So, watch this space on that one. But as of yet, we’re not commercialising Thomson as a thing you can buy.”

Innovating faster

Computer Weekly last spoke with Roth in summer 2025, when she outlined her mission to transform internal processes and customer services using digital systems and services. That process, which involves ensuring high-quality AI is used internally and in the firm’s products, has sped up during the past 12 months, especially with the launch of Thomson.

“The way that we can build products now means, yes, we still have people involved, of course, but we can have AI write a large amount of our codebase,” she says.

“We’re releasing stuff far more quickly, so that’s exciting. But that pace comes with a whole bunch of implications. And then the work level across all teams typically goes up.”

Roth describes the past 12 months as busy. However, there’s no let-up in the pace of digital transformation in the age of AI. She recognises that a development like Thomson helps her firm stay one step ahead of its rivals.

“Our competition is also innovating faster than ever, so that threat keeps it sporty,” she says.

One area where this rivalry could extend in the future is in model development. Roth expects other firms to follow her pioneering lead and to launch LLMs. The CIOs she meets are often worried about spiralling AI costs. Developing your own model gives you control of your own destiny. However, model development, given the expense, won’t be right for everyone.

“You’ve got to believe that the data you have is going to give you an advantage,” she says.

“Otherwise you’re going to create something that’s probably not as good and still costs you some money. There’s got to be some commercial differentiator in there, which we believe our content gives us.”

Financial information provider Thomson Reuters has developed an in-house, proprietary large language model (LLM) to power its use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the products it develops for customers.

Senior executives in most major enterprises are turning to generative and agentic AI to explore value-generating opportunities – but significant challenges, such as security, accuracy and fears over supplier lock-in, can prevent firms from making the most of such opportunities.

In a pioneering attempt to overcome these issues, content and technology specialist Thomson Reuters has taken a step that would be anathema to many CIOs and their C-suite colleagues – launching its own in-house-developed proprietary LLM.

Kirsty Roth, chief operating officer at Thomson Reuters, understands that many of her digital leadership peers would see the company’s decision to launch its LLM, known as Thomson, as radical. Tech giants, such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, spend billions of dollars developing new models on what feels like a weekly release cadence.

AI model development is a world characterised by rapid change and high investment, so why would a traditional blue-chip enterprise outside the high-tech world of super-powerful frontier models decide to spend millions of dollars developing its own LLM? After all, aren’t the tech giants always going to be bigger and better at AI?

Not necessarily, suggests Roth. Yes, the behemoths will have the edge in developing publicly available models, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, that a broad user base can explore and exploit for day-to-day activities across a range of industries and professions.

“The big tech companies are always going to be bigger, and I think potentially better for very generic use cases,” she says.

title: Executive interview: Reckitt has no fear of missing out on the AI frenzy
raw_text:
Bastien Parizot, senior vice-president of global business services and artificial intelligence (AI) at hygiene and consumer health brands parent Reckitt, remains level-headed when it comes to the latest developments in technology. For him, fear of missing out is one of the enemies of AI adoption.

“I think there is a lot changing in the world of AI outside,” says Parizot.

Rather than chasing all of the new shiny tech, he believes IT and business leaders should change the way people work to deploy AI at scale across their organisations.

“I don’t like the words ‘AI strategy’ because we only have one strategy, which is a business one,” says Parizot. “We believe we have an AI approach which enables the business strategy.”

Given the pace of change across the tech landscape, particularly in terms of how quickly AI is evolving, he says a company like Reckitt – which owns brands like Cillit Bang, Durex, Dettol and Nurofen – is not concerned about having access to the latest AI. Instead, he says: “Our business is actually to make sure we put better health in the hands of consumers every day.

“AI should be an enabler to help people do their jobs better,” says Parizot. “We shouldn’t be chasing the latest models, otherwise, I would have shifted through maybe eight models in the past two years. The reality is that we bring value by having AI enabling our core businesses and the processes within the enterprise.”

He says the goal of enterprise AI is to deliver business value. This means moving beyond testing and piloting artificial intelligence and delivering AI projects that scale.

AI in R&D

In May, Parizot, along with chief research and development officer Angela Naef, gave a presentation showing digital science at the company. Among the digital technologies presented was a generative AI tool called WriteItt, a good practice (GxP)-compliant AI platform for document drafting, literature search, and protocol generation.

GxP is a framework and guidance for life science and healthcare. “Validating our system as GxP-compliant ensures further robustness, repeatability and continuous control with strong data integrity and high product quality at the centre,” says Parizot. 

Rather than building WriteItt using a generic AI tool layered onto the business, he says it was co-developed with the respective teams in R&D and designed around process reinvention of real workflows.

“Much of the discussion around AI focuses on the technology and performance of large language models,” says Parizot. “Our effort has been on putting AI to work by codifying the tacit knowledge of our teams into AI applications.”

It also embeds context around market categories and Reckitt-specific information. “Applying this approach at scale and consistently across all teams is where we believe AI makes a real difference in driving our winning playbook,” he says.

Looking at how WriteItt works in industrial trials, Parizot says: “Every time we scale a product from the labs to the factory, teams must prepare, review and approve detailed industrial trial reports across category teams, product development teams, quality and supply.

“We run more than 250 of these trials each year across brands, including Lysol and Vanish. With WriteItt, drafting and reviewing become significantly faster – up to eight times faster – which means our teams are spending far fewer hours creating documents and much more time on advancing innovation.”

  • Putting a value on open source: Spotify’s open source tech lead discusses why open source is failing those whose free time is dedicated to maintaining code.

WriteItt is one of many AI projects helping to support the business. In fact, Reckitt started embedding AI into a transformation that began in the summer of 2024. The company worked with Boston Consulting Group (BCG) and its technology arm, BCG X, on a programme that has enabled Reckitt to modernise key parts of its business.

From a technology perspective, Reckitt has implemented an enterprise-wide AI platform it calls Trinity AI, which brings together different datasets and types of databases as well as AI models, all accessible via managed application programming interfaces.

According to a BCG LinkedIn post, hundreds of teams are using custom AI tools and 40% of employee time has been freed for higher-value work.

In the company’s latest financial results, filed at the end of July 2026, chief financial officer Shannon Eisenhard was asked about the company’s AI investment and IT costs. She said Reckitt was very focused on driving AI across the company.

“We view it as something that’s not only going to enable us to drive productivity, which we’ve talked a lot about, but we also view it as a tool that’s going to help us drive top-line growth, and so we’re very focused on making sure that we’re expanding and focusing on both sides of the equation.”

Looking specifically at token cost, which correlates to how much AI workloads actually cost the business, she said: “We just reviewed it and it’s very small today. We’re assuming it will grow quite rapidly, but even assuming that rapid growth, we don’t see it as something that we’re particularly concerned about at this point in time.”

She said Reckitt is investing heavily in building internal models and capabilities to deliver productivity as well as top-line growth.

An iterative journey

Parizot describes the company’s experience of AI as “a continuous learning journey”. It has used AI to create more content, but he says this may not be how the technology is used a year from now.

While there is no fear of missing out, he says: “We are constantly reassessing the complete return on investment of what we’re doing by domain.”

Reckitt relies on its technology partners to help it build the technology to achieve favourable business outcomes, but Parizot says the key to a successful business outcome is not linked to a particular technology or technology partner.

“It’s our ability to change the ways we work, our ability to bring a consistent way of doing things so that we are being more effective and can change how the business operates,” he says.

For Parizot, regardless of the technology, data and knowledge management codifies the know-how people have and helps everyone across the business access that knowledge.

title: Dreamforce 2026: Marc Benioff beats customer data drum for business AI use
raw_text:
Amid a surge in public discourse about artificial intelligence (AI) killing all humans within a decade, Marc Benioff, chairman and CEO of Salesforce (pictured), told attendees of the software supplier’s Dreamforce conference in San Francisco that its approach to AI is grounded in the more mundane reality of its customers’ data.

The supplier is introducing AIforce at the event, described as a management layer and toolkit for the “headless” version of its customer relationship management (CRM) software, which it calls Headless 360. In enterprise software, “headless” typically means separating the user interface from the data or other content that sits on the back end of the application.

The supplier is enabling users of its CRM software to work through Anthropic’s Claude AI model or the Slack teams messaging technology it acquired in 2020.

At the event, the supplier disclosed more details about Claudeforce, a collaboration that makes hundreds of Salesforce features available within Anthropic’s Claude AI model. The Claudeforce plugin will be available in public beta to joint Salesforce and Claude customers, said Patrick Stokes, president of applications and marketing at Salesforce, in a pre-conference press briefing.

With AIforce, the supplier said in a press statement, it is bringing all the enterprise knowledge inside Salesforce – the data, workflows, business logic, semantics, permissions, security and governance that already run the business – to any AI interface. It claimed that, as a result, companies can unlock business value from all the knowledge already inside Salesforce, bringing trusted context and governance into any agentic productivity tool.

Benioff said in the statement: “AI is creating an interface revolution. We are combining model intelligence with all the context that customers have built into Salesforce to create an intelligent, dynamic, composable system that is securely governed, built with zero data retention, and designed to work with the core systems that already run your business.”

More informally, in a post-keynote press “scrum”, Benioff added another dimension of context when talking about his recent travels in the supplier’s market.

Having spent the previous two months in Europe, he said that his time in European countries, including the UK, had revealed to him the uneven development of AI globally. There were no self-driving Waymo cars in sight, he lamented.

“I spent a huge amount of time in Germany,” he said. “We have great customers there, including Siemens, Mercedes and Volkswagen.”

But in respect of AI adoption, he said Europe was “not as far along” as the US.

“I think the example of the Waymo, common in San Francisco, is a metaphor. There’s a spectrum where maybe Shanghai is the furthest along. I don’t think that they [the Europeans] are way behind. But I think that there’s a spectrum. And I think in the next year or two, we’ll see all these countries kind of catch up.”

On the other hand, more positively, he reported in the keynote that one customer, based in Lausanne, Switzerland, said they appreciated the supplier’s approach to AI as unlocking “trapped value” within existing data.

The supplier said AIforce makes AI interfaces “intelligent and dynamic”, meaning that agents can reason across all the data, logic and conversations in Salesforce at once, “surfacing insights instead of records to sort through”.

It also said it makes any AI interfaces “secure and governed” because “every request runs on existing permissions and business rules, every agent sees only what the person asking can see, and every action routes back” through the supplier’s software.

Additionally, AIforce can, it said, make interfaces composable, so that “anyone can build an interface, agent or view, built on trusted data and business logic, simply by describing it – with MCPs, APIs, plug-ins, and skills for teams that want to go further”.

title: Advice for CIOs on AI’s 'existential threat'
raw_text:
The US president has dismissed posts by the CEOs of OpenAI and Anthropic calling for an artificial intelligence (AI) slowdown as hoaxes, while Meta’s boss continues to push the line that AI is the future of humanity. However, in light of greater public scrutiny over AI safety, IT leaders may be asked if their AI strategy is likely to change following these latest remarks.

Over the weekend, following the latest update to the Claude Mythos security breach, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for the development of frontier AI models to be paced. “Like many technologies before it, AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious,” he said.

“Over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence – not just investing in risk prevention, but pacing the rate of capabilities advancement so that risk prevention has time to keep up. We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” he added.

Amodei noted that AI has been advancing drastically faster, driven primarily by its ability to build the next generation of AI itself.

On Tuesday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman tweeted on X: “The world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especially as the trajectory of progress has steepened. Every frontier lab must deliver on this, and there is no reason any of us should come to work if we cannot.”

He claimed that OpenAI was excited to have independent audits of its frontier models. “We welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI. But we do not believe we need to wait for an antitrust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence. Consistent rules to manage frontier risk so that we can maximise the benefits are a good idea,” said Altman.

These remarks follow on from various studies exploring AI’s risk to humanity. An MIT FutureTech report based on a Delphi Study of 272 international experts warned of existential risks ranging from AI generating misinformation that undermines society, environmental impact and job losses, to cyber attacks and weapons that use AI brains. The experts judged there to be a more than 10% chance of catastrophic outcomes over the next five years.

One area that is often overlooked is what the experts in the Delphi Study categorise as the “power centralisation risk”. This is where the same entities developing AI are often best positioned to capture its benefits, creating self-reinforcing dynamics that are difficult to reverse through technical interventions alone.

In August, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates warned of the risks of AI, looking specifically at the wealth divide. “AI will either be the greatest equaliser ever invented, or the worst source of injustice,” he said. “The challenge is monumental. How will we use this technology to make the world a fairer place and keep it from widening the divide between rich and poor? How will we protect the people who are most vulnerable to the harms it causes?”

Read more about AI safety

  • Will AI ruin society? In the same week that Nvidia posted yet another record quarter, Bill Gates, co-founder of Microsoft, issued a warning about artificial intelligence. 
  • The AI safety crunch and how enterprises should deal with it: The competitive landscape, particularly the geopolitical clash between the US and China, complicates the AI safety dilemma.

A shift in attitude

Arun Chandrasekaran, distinguished vice-president analyst at Gartner, described the call from AI chiefs to address the safety of frontier AI models as requiring a shift in enterprise thinking from agility to AI agility with safety.

“CIOs should prioritise proven use cases while strengthening AI governance, evaluation, security, observability and human oversight. CIOs and CISOs need to define their own end-to-end AI safety guardrails that are use case-specific,” he said, adding that these should strongly complement the guardrails provided by AI technology providers.

And last week – before the Amodei and Altman posts – Boston Consulting Group stated that the desire to move fast on AI without putting appropriate risk management in place can result in a system lapse or use cases being deployed in areas with strong regulatory requirements that organisations are unprepared for.

“That’s a serious business liability and could ultimately lead to an erosion of customer trust,” Steve Mills, managing director and partner at BCG, warned. He described AI governance as “a huge business unlock, not just a bottleneck” because it enables organisations to focus resources on the use cases that can deliver the most value as well as manage the risk.

Given that AI governance can be used as a criterion for choosing the best projects to take forward, Gartner’s Chandrasekaran urged CIOs to continue speaking to their business chiefs about funding AI initiatives with measurable business value. “Build optionality into AI strategies through modular architectures, multiple model providers, strong evaluation and the ability to rapidly change models as capabilities and risks evolve,” he said.

One factor CIOs will need to consider if guardrails slow down the pace of frontier model development is that the financial markets are betting that AI growth will continue to accelerate. If this sentiment changes, some AI companies may find their funding diminish.

Daniel Turgel, partner and co-head of White & Case’s global technology industry group, said: “If spending expectations soften, the implications could be significant, extending beyond AI developers to chipmakers, energy providers and infrastructure businesses. Greater investor selectivity could also accelerate consolidation, as businesses with stronger balance sheets acquire technology from less well-capitalised competitors.”

In spite of rival companies calling for a slowdown in the development of frontier AI models, Meta’s CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, has so far remained silent, and his company remains committed to pushing forward AI developments.

AI, according to Zuckerberg, represents the future of humanity. He has promised “superintelligence” on Meta’s social media platform. “American communities will have greater prosperity and security if America and its allies lead in AI compared to geopolitical rivals,” he said.

This viewpoint is aligned with that of the current US administration. US president Donald Trump has previously stated: “The USA is the leader in AI and our administration plans to keep it that way.” 

Responding to the warnings of Altman and Amodei, Trump posted on his social media platform, Truth Social: “Concerning AI, when, in the history of business, did anyone see the leaders of an industry call for regulation that, if strongly implemented, will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy? AI taking over the world, destroying humanity, and all other things bad, is a hoax.”

title: CW@60: The splice of life – how much has changed, and yet how little
raw_text:
On 22 September 2026, Computer Weekly turns 60. To mark the milestone, we asked some of our friends - experts, parliamentarians, IT leaders and suppliers - for their perspectives on how tech has changed their lives over six decades. What's changed the most for you since then?

Looking from the perspective of not long away from the big day - and apologies for falling into self-reverence as a member of the team - happy 60th birthday to Computer Weekly. These days, someone being in their sixties and still able to do all of the things they’ve done for decades has become somewhat normalised. In the world of publishing, this is very much far from the case. Getting to 60 is quite the achievement.

And to indulge oneself a bit, from the perspective of a career in technology journalism that is almost celebrating 40 years, it’s very much a personal achievement be onboard the good ship Computer Weekly to celebrate this momentous occasion.

Almost 40 years ago, while beginning a working life in the depths of a petrochemical giant’s research laboratory, the very idea of writing anything other than rather basic Fortran 77 code (no pun intended) for investigating car engine performance was the realm of fiction.

Two years earlier- with the pinnacle of my prose being badly put together reports about maximising signals on fused optical-fibre loops (if, for once, not broken) – doing “writing” for a magazine that for all of my professional life has been a market leader was almost literally unthinkable.

But such memories are rather telling - and also offered in their own way glimpses of the future for networking and communications, if not just for me personally in a laboratory.

Stutter and pinging

For example, investigating car engine performance is still a core part of the job these days. Not as it was then by looking how different formulations of the latest new-fangled petrol worked on engines and phenomena like stutter, pinging and hesitation. These days it’s all about electrification and the connected vehicle and software-defined vehicles in general which are redefining the auto industry.

As for fibre, this has evolved from a former source of fury due to the use of a massively temperamental autoclave to fuse multi- to single-mode optical cables. Obviously not for any user shortcomings. Oh no. How the machinery survived a rather testing research project for the whole of the summer of 1987 remains a mystery.

“2026 also marks 150 years since the first telephone call by Alexander Graham Bell. It’s fair to say that everything has changed since then, on a technical and societal basis”

Joe O’Halloran

What isn’t a mystery is the effect that (properly working) optical-fibre networks have had on businesses and homes throughout the UK. Nobody could envisage 10 years ago, never mind 39, that homes could gain access to optical-fibre comms offering potential throughput of 10Gbps, as is the case with XGS-PON right now.

And to imagine then a time where the talk is of counting down to 95% of the UK having access to such connectivity. That’s just good for every business and household.

And on another personal note, I have seen with my own eyes – and felt with my own not-so-nimble fingers – how optical-fibre engineering and technology has evolved from a maintenance and set-up perspective. On a visit to a research lab belonging to one leading service provider, the once-infuriated hapless research student of the 1980s was able to fuse fibres accurately within seconds not days. And if I can do it after such a time gap, then just think what today’s talented comms industry field engineers can do.

First call

Yet looking at today’s networking and communications industry, it’s not just Computer Weekly that is blowing out the candles for a landmark birthday - 2026 also marks the milestone of 150 years since the first telephone call by Alexander Graham Bell.

It’s fair to say that everything has changed since then, on a technical and societal basis. The voice call invention of 1876 seems as revolutionary as AI-run networks – especially chatbot journeys – do now. It’s somewhat tempting to wonder what the Edinburgh-born inventor would make of his nearby Royal & Ancient golf course’s recent investment in AI-based critical networking infrastructure.

It’s also 180 years since the UK’s Electric Telegraph Company was founded as the world's first public telegraph enterprise. After being taken over by the British government under the auspices of the General Post Office in 1870, the company we now know as BT has left an indelible mark on the country’s communications infrastructure.

Happy birthday and also congratulations to one and all in comms. Long may you all continue to innovate and shape our lives.
